passages.t: Damascus a heap of ruins, and gleanings left in Israel
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Damascus’ (verse 1). Damascus will no longer be a city; it will become a heap of ruins. The cities of Aroer will be left to flocks (verse 2). ‘The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the sovereignty from Damascus’ (verse 3), and what is left of Aram will be like the faded splendor of Israel.

‘In that day the splendor of Jacob will fade, and the fat of his body will waste away’ (verse 4). It will be like a field after the reapers, like gleaning grain in the Valley of Rephaim (verse 5). ‘Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten’ (verse 6): two or three berries at the top, four or five on its branches.
passages.hearers:
The oracles turn north. Damascus, capital of Aram, had joined the northern kingdom of Israel to pressure Judah in the crisis of chapters 7 and 8. Isaiah had told Ahaz not to fear these two smoldering stubs. Chapter 17 makes the same point as an oracle, and puts Israel, called Ephraim and Jacob, inside an oracle addressed to a foreign nation. The people of God who allied with a pagan power will fall with it.

In the 730s BC Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel formed an alliance against Assyria. Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC, killed Rezin and deported its people, turning Aram into Assyrian provinces. He also stripped Israel of Galilee and the land east of the Jordan, and ten years later Samaria fell. The oracle likely comes from shortly before 732 BC.

The first hearers knew harvest. Reapers took the standing grain, and the poor gleaned what was left. Olive trees were beaten with sticks to bring down the fruit, leaving only a few berries at the top. Israel will be like that: almost nothing left, but not nothing. The gleanings are the remnant.

The cities of Aroer are puzzling, since the best-known Aroer lay in Moab, far to the south. Some scholars think the name refers to towns under Aram's control; others follow a different reading in the Greek translation.
passages.later: Kings records how it happened: the king of Assyria ‘marched up to Damascus, and captured it. He took its people to Kir as captives and put Rezin to death’ (2 Kings 16:9).
passages.hard:
Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Has verse 1 been fulfilled?

Interpreters answer in different ways. Many hold that the prophecy was fulfilled in 732 BC, when Tiglath-pileser III captured Damascus, killed its king, deported its people and ended its independence. Verse 3 speaks of sovereignty removed from Damascus, which is exactly what happened. On this view, heap of ruins is the ordinary language of conquest in ancient prophecy and inscriptions, describing a capital destroyed as a kingdom, not a site never lived on again. Some readers, noting that Damascus was rebuilt and thrives, argue that verse 1 still awaits a future destruction, a view common in some popular prophecy teaching. Others see a partial fulfillment in the eighth century pointing toward God's final judgment on all powers that oppose him.

The text's own horizon is the Aram and Israel of Isaiah's day, tied to the crisis of chapter 7, and that is the place to begin. These notes do not read this verse as a prediction about any war, city or nation of the present day.
passages.asks: Israel allied with Damascus and fell with it. Ask what alliances you have made that tie your future to people who do not share your faith. And ask what it means that God promises gleanings even after the harvest is gone.

passages.t: Looking to their Maker, and the forgotten Rock
passages.happening:
‘In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 7). They will not look to the altars they made with their hands, or to the Asherah poles and incense altars made by their fingers (verse 8).

In that day their strong cities will be like abandoned thickets (verse 9). ‘For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge’ (verse 10). So though they plant pleasant gardens and set out cuttings from foreign vines, and make them sprout the very morning they plant (verses 10-11), ‘yet the harvest will vanish on the day of disease and incurable pain’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Judgment has a purpose. In that day people will turn from the things they made to the one who made them. The altars and Asherah poles were the trappings of Canaanite worship that Israel had taken up. Asherah was a goddess, and her pole stood for her.

The pleasant gardens and foreign cuttings of verses 10 and 11 may point to gardens used in the fertility cults of the region. Others take them simply as a picture of Israel's investment in foreign alliances and ways. Either way, the picture is of energy poured into what cannot last, while the Rock is forgotten.

The first hearers would have known the title Rock from Moses' song, where God is the Rock whose work is perfect.
passages.later: Moses sang, ‘He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just’ (Deuteronomy 32:4). And David sang, ‘The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer’ (Psalm 18:2).
passages.asks: The people forgot the Rock of their refuge and planted gardens that could not last. Ask what you are cultivating with great care that will not survive a hard day. And ask what you have made with your own hands that you look to instead of your Maker.

passages.t: The nations roar, and are gone by morning
passages.happening:
‘Alas, the tumult of many peoples; they rage like the roaring seas’ (verse 12). They rumble like crashing waters. ‘The nations rage like the rush of many waters. He rebukes them, and they flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale’ (verse 13).

“In the evening, there is sudden terror! Before morning, they are no more!” (verse 14). ‘This is the portion of those who loot us and the lot of those who plunder us’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These verses look beyond the crisis with Damascus to a pattern: the nations raging against God's people and being driven away. The roaring sea was the ancient picture of chaos. God rebukes it, and it flees.

The picture of terror in the evening and nothing left by morning will be acted out when Assyria besieges Jerusalem in chapters 36 and 37, and its army is struck in a single night. The first hearers were being prepared to trust that the armies roaring at their gates were not the last word.
passages.later: A psalm sings the same: ‘Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice’ (Psalm 46:6). And Isaiah later tells how ‘the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (Isaiah 37:36).
passages.asks: The nations roar like the sea, and by morning they are gone. Ask what roaring threat keeps you awake. And ask whether you can trust the one who rebukes the sea when the sea is loudest.
